tagline.text: Giant papier-mâché figures and water blessings on the streets of Angono

location.label: Location
location.text: Angono, Rizal — around M.L. Quezon Avenue and the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of St. Clement

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Mid-November to the 23rd (events continue into December and beyond)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: Approx. ₱500~1,500 (day trip from Manila, per person)

children.text: The Higantes Festival is a parade of giant papier-mâché figures held every November in Angono, Rizal, alongside the town fiesta honoring St. Clement, the patron saint of fishermen. Hundreds of giants and the basaan water dousing are the highlights.

The Higantes Festival is one of the best-known street festivals in the Philippines, held in Angono, a lakeside town in Rizal province east of Manila. Higante is Spanish for "giant," and the festival's figures are large papier-mâché puppets about 3 m tall, carried on parade by a person standing inside. Angono times the festival to the feast day of its patron saint, St. Clement (San Clemente), which falls on
November 23
. Major events therefore cluster around that date, and the feast Mass is held at the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of St. Clement in Angono.

The tradition dates back to the Spanish colonial era. Angono was then hacienda land, and the landowners reportedly forbade villagers from gathering except at one festival a year. The story goes that villagers used the papier-mâché technique learned from Spanish friars to make giant caricature puppets mocking the landowners and paraded them on that day. Today most higantes have human faces, and some villages work their local specialty into the head design. For example, a village known for ducks and balut is said to field a duck-headed higante.

Besides the giants, the parade includes a marching band and the parehadores, young girls in wooden slippers who carry paddles (sagwan). They shout "Viva, San Clemente!" in honor of the saint. Since water is the festival's symbol, fitting for the patron saint of fishermen, there is also the custom of basaan, in which people douse one another with water during the parade. Getting wet is regarded as a blessing. Villages now build their own puppets and sometimes compete, and the number of giants in the parade runs into the hundreds.

The festival period changes every year. The 2026 festival was announced with an official program running from October 30 to Angono Day on January 1, 2027, and the Grand Parade of higantes was held on Sunday, November 15. Because the Grand Parade and the feast-day events can fall on different dates, be sure to check the official schedule for the year you plan to go. Angono's art town itself is covered in its own separate entry.
Giants more than 3 m tall, each made by a village, file along M.L. Quezon Avenue. The 2026 Grand Parade set off from SM Center Angono at
on
November 15
, and about 300 giants were reported to have taken part.

People douse one another with water as a blessing. In some places water is thrown from windows or sprayed with hoses, so you can be soaked within minutes. Be sure to bring a change of clothes and a waterproof pouch.
On the feast day itself,
November 23
at
, the town fiesta Mass is held at the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of St. Clement in Angono. It is the most traditional moment of the festival, when local parishioners gather.

blocks.title: Fluvial Procession on Laguna de Bay

children.text: On the afternoon of the feast day, a fluvial procession is said to carry the image of St. Clement on a decorated boat across Laguna de Bay. However, the official program gives no time for it, and it depends on tides and weather, so confirm with the tourism office.

blocks.title: The Craft of Making the Giants

children.text: The head is made by pasting many layers of newspaper strips and takes about a week. The body is woven from bamboo or rattan strips so it can be carried for hours. Building a single figure is said to take about a month.
Angono is famous for itik (duck) dishes, and during the festival there are fried duck and local cooking contests. Street food such as fishballs and barbecue is also sold around the parade route.

True to its reputation as an artists' town, Angono holds painting contests, exhibitions, performances and music events in November and December. In 2026, a photo exhibit was held at SM Center Angono and an arts festival at the gymnasium.

items.title: Grand Parade Day Route
items.subtitle: From early morning to evening fireworks

children.text: Leave Manila early and arrive near SM Center Angono. Roads are closed on parade day, so aim to arrive around
, use the restroom beforehand and pick a spot along the route toward the municipal hall.
The parade sets off from SM Center Angono. Keep some distance as the giants pass, and be ready to get splashed.
Cheering contests and street dance performances continue along M.L. Quezon Avenue. The 2026 program listed the higantes cheer at
and a stop dance at
Have lunch at the fried duck stalls on M. Diaz Street or the itik lane beside the gymnasium. It gets crowded, so go early.
In the evening, fireworks and a music night follow on the avenue. Return transport is crowded, so agree on a meeting point with your group.
Times are based on the official 2026 program and may change each year, so check the latest announcements from the Angono tourism office.

items.title: Feast Day (November 23) Route
items.subtitle: Mass, fluvial procession and a stroll around town

children.text: Attend the feast-day Mass at the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of St. Clement, or simply take in the atmosphere around the church.
Walk around the church and M.L. Quezon Avenue to enjoy the town, then head toward the lakeshore to see the preparations for the fluvial procession.
After lunch, visit the galleries and street reliefs of Angono Art Town. Check in advance whether private galleries are open.
If the fluvial procession takes place in the afternoon, watch it from the lakeshore. The time may change depending on tides and weather.
Basaan may continue on the feast day too, so be prepared for water.

29 km

12 km

UV Express vans and jeepneys run to Angono from places such as Cubao and EDSA Shaw. One guide listed fares of about
from Cubao and EDSA Shaw.
During festival periods, drivers sometimes charge special fares, so confirm the fare before boarding.
Travel time varies greatly with traffic. It is usually about
1 to 1.5 hours
, but some visitors report trips of up to
2.5 hours
when leaving after the early morning on parade day.
Fares and routes can change, so confirm locally.
Buses from Cubao or EDSA Shaw toward Binangonan or Angono are said to drop you near the town center.
Because roads into Angono get blocked during the festival, be prepared to walk after getting off the bus.
By car, take Ortigas Avenue Extension or Marcos Highway and join Manila East Road.
One guide says that on the November 15 parade day, roads into Angono were closed from
, with a detour (Baytown Road to Manila East Road) announced. Confirm exact closure times and sections with Angono Tourism.
Parking at SM Center Angono is reportedly about
, and from there you walk or take a tricycle to the parade route. Parking space is limited.
The town center is walkable. For longer distances, take a tricycle.
Roads along the parade route are closed. Tricycles may also have trouble getting in.
The core of the Higantes Festival is November. In 2026 the Grand Parade was held on November 15, and the feast of St. Clement is
November 23
. The two may not fall on the same day, so decide first which event you want to see.
November is the start of the dry season and relatively cool, but the midday parade route is hot under the sun. A sudden shower is also possible, so bring a rain jacket and a towel.

Rooms in Angono fill up quickly around the Grand Parade, so most visitors make a day trip from Manila or Antipolo. If you want to stay in town, book early; if you live nearby, it is easiest to arrive early in the morning and head home before the evening rush.

Duck (itik) dishes are Angono's pride. Fried duck is sold on M. Diaz Street and in the itik lane beside the gymnasium. The Balaw-Balaw restaurant on Doña Justa Street is known for exotic local dishes such as coconut worms and traditional stews, and booking ahead is wise during the festival. There are also seafood restaurants along the lakeshore for a casual meal.
On Grand Parade day, arrive early (around
) to claim a spot. The good places on the steps along the route fill up around
Put your phone in a waterproof pouch, and bring spare clothes and a towel. You can be drenched by the basaan.
Wear closed, flat shoes that will not slip off. Wet asphalt is slippery.
Bring plenty of cash and small bills. Visitors have reported that the ATM near the plaza ran out early.
Public restrooms are scarce, so use the ones at SM Center Angono beforehand.
Agree on a meeting point with your group in advance. Some visitors report that mobile data dropped for a while in the crowds.
Check announcements from the Angono tourism office and the Angono municipal government's Facebook pages. The schedule changes often.
Adding a visit to Angono Art Town's galleries or the petroglyphs makes for a fuller day.
On Grand Parade day, roads into Angono are closed from early morning and crowds are huge, so plan on public transport and walking.
The person carrying a higante has limited visibility and a heavy load, so do not crowd the figures and keep a safe distance.
Alcohol sales are reportedly restricted and drinking on the streets prohibited along the event area. Check the latest announcements for the rules.
Drones require prior coordination. Do not fly one on your own.
A local ordinance reportedly bans single-use plastics and Styrofoam, so bring your own containers.
Watch out for pickpockets and loss, and keep valuables close to your body.
In an emergency, contact the Angono MDRRMO at (02) 542-1772, the police at (02) 651-0061, or the tourism office at (02) 661-3646, though numbers can change.
The festival town is itself a home of painters and sculptors. Walk around its galleries and street reliefs.
